chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Fed at the Center

lessons.title: From Fed Policy to Dalal Street: Rate Differentials, Carry Trades, and FPI Flows

body.text: A Fed rate decision does not reach the Nifty through "sentiment." It travels through a specific chain: US yields move, the interest rate differential between India and the US changes, the profitability of carrying rupee assets changes, and FPI positioning in Indian debt and equity adjusts accordingly.

children.text: The transmission chain runs in a fixed order. The Fed changes its policy rate or its guidance about future rates. US Treasury yields, especially the 2-year and 10-year, move in response. The gap between Indian and US yields, the interest rate differential, widens or narrows. That differential changes how attractive it is to borrow in a low-yield currency and hold higher-yielding rupee assets, the carry trade. Finally, FPI flows into or out of Indian government securities and equities adjust, and the rupee and the Nifty move as a consequence, not as the starting point.
The Carry Trade, in One Formula

body.caption: Where i(INR) and i(USD) are the interest rates available in each currency, and delta-s is the percentage depreciation of the rupee against the dollar over the holding period. The trade is profitable only if the rate differential earned is larger than the rupee's depreciation over that period.

children.text: This is why a widening India-US rate differential, on its own, tends to draw FPI money into Indian debt, and a narrowing differential tends to push it back out, all else being equal. The phrase "all else being equal" is doing a lot of work here, and the rest of this lesson is about what happens when it does not hold.

body.title: Find the Breakeven Depreciation
body.prompt: INR interest rates are 7% and USD interest rates are 5%. What annual rupee depreciation against the dollar, in percent, would exactly wipe out the carry advantage?
body.explanation: The carry advantage is the differential itself: 7% minus 5% equals 2%. If the rupee depreciates by more than 2% against the dollar over the holding period, the currency loss exceeds the extra interest earned, and the carry trade becomes unprofitable, even though the interest rate differential looked attractive at the start.

body.label: India-US 10-Year Yield Spread, Pre-2022 vs 2023
body.context: As the Fed hiked aggressively through 2022 and 2023 while India's own rate rise was more measured, the spread compressed to among its narrowest levels in decades, by widely cited market commentary. Approximate figures; check current G-Sec and US Treasury yields directly.

body.text: A compressed rate differential should, by the simple carry logic above, have pushed FPI debt money out of India. It did not happen that way. Structural flows can override the simple carry story, and reading only the interest rate differential without checking for these structural flows is a common analytical mistake.

children.text: Case Study: Index Inclusion Overrides the Carry Story

body.title: How Index Inclusion Drew Money In Despite a Narrow Spread

events.title: Fed Hikes Aggressively
events.description: The Fed's fastest hiking cycle in decades compresses the India-US rate differential sharply, which by the simple carry logic should discourage FPI debt inflows.

events.title: JPMorgan Announces India's Inclusion in the GBI-EM Index
events.description: JPMorgan announces that Indian government bonds will be added to its widely tracked GBI-EM Global Diversified bond index, with India's weight set to rise gradually toward roughly 10% over time.

events.title: Inclusion Takes Effect
events.description: As the inclusion phases in, index-tracking global bond funds are structurally required to buy Indian government securities regardless of the prevailing rate differential, drawing in FPI debt inflows even with a historically narrow India-US spread.

body.text: Dates, spread figures, and index weight targets above are approximate and drawn from widely reported market coverage. Confirm current figures with JPMorgan's index methodology and NSDL's FPI debt flow data before using them in analysis.

children.text: It is also worth separating debt flows from equity flows, since a retail investor on Zerodha mostly experiences the equity side. FPI debt flows are the most directly sensitive to the rate differential and carry logic above, because a bond's return is close to its yield. FPI equity flows into the NSE and BSE respond to the rate differential too, but they are also driven by earnings growth, risk appetite, and the general direction of global liquidity covered in Chapter 1. A narrow rate differential can coincide with strong FPI equity inflows if India's growth and earnings outlook is strong enough to offset a smaller carry cushion, which is exactly why professionals track debt and equity FPI flows separately rather than treating "FPI flows" as one undifferentiated number.

body.title: Debt Says One Thing, Equity Says Another
body.scenario: You notice that FPI debt flows into Indian government securities have turned negative for the month, consistent with a narrowing India-US rate differential. In the same month, FPI equity flows into the NSE and BSE are strongly positive.
body.prompt: Is this a contradiction? What would you check before concluding that the liquidity backdrop for India is either clearly tightening or clearly loosening?
body.modelAnswer: This is not necessarily a contradiction, because debt and equity FPI flows respond to different drivers. The negative debt flow is consistent with the compressed rate differential making the pure carry trade less attractive. The positive equity flow could reflect index inclusion related buying, strong earnings momentum, or a broader risk-on shift in global liquidity that favors equities specifically. Before concluding anything about the overall liquidity backdrop, you would want to check whether the equity inflow is broad-based across sectors (a genuine risk-on signal) or concentrated in specific large index constituents (more consistent with passive, structural buying), and whether global proxies like DXY and FRA-OIS from Chapter 1 confirm a loosening or a tightening bias.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: Why did FPI debt inflows into India increase in 2024 even though the India-US interest rate differential had compressed to historically narrow levels?
options: Because the RBI banned FPI equity investment, forcing money into debt
Because India's GDP growth alone made bonds attractive regardless of yield
Because index inclusion in JPMorgan's GBI-EM index created structural, rate-differential-independent buying from index-tracking funds
Because the rupee appreciated so much that carry losses became irrelevant
body.explanation: Structural, benchmark-driven flows from index inclusion do not depend on the carry trade being attractive. Funds that track the GBI-EM index are required to hold Indian bonds in proportion to India's index weight, which can override what the simple interest rate differential would otherwise predict.

points: Fed policy reaches Indian markets through a specific chain: US yields move, the India-US rate differential changes, carry trade profitability changes, and FPI flows adjust accordingly.
The carry trade is only profitable if the rate differential earned is larger than the rupee's depreciation against the dollar over the holding period.
A compressed rate differential does not mechanically guarantee FPI outflows; structural flows like index inclusion can override the simple carry logic.
FPI debt flows are more directly sensitive to the rate differential than FPI equity flows, which also respond to earnings, risk appetite, and the broader global liquidity backdrop.
Reading FPI flows well means checking debt and equity flows separately, and checking whether a flow is broad-based or driven by structural, index-related buying.
